title: Chaos Monkey for LLM Safety: Probing Guardrails with Controlled Fault Injection

original_idea.quick_reasoning: Clearly addresses an AI Safety problem with a reasonably scoped approach.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Clear chain: real deployments have degraded conditions (truncated prompts, garbled context). If safety fails under degraded conditions, the lab-to-deployment gap is quantified and specific failure modes are identified. Directly actionable for deployment hardening.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Implementing random perturbations to prompt components (truncation, noise injection) before API calls is straightforward scripting. Measuring safety degradation uses existing scoring tools. Accessible to beginners with basic Python.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Clear deliverable: safety degradation curve as a function of chaos intensity for a specific model. Single experiment with well-defined metric. Achievable in 30 hours if perturbation types are bounded.

novelty.reasoning: 'Assessing and Enhancing the Robustness of LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems Through Chaos Engineering' (arXiv:2505.03096, 2025) applies chaos engineering to LLM-based multi-agent systems, injecting faults to test robustness. ChaosEater (arXiv:2511.07865, 2025) automates the chaos engineering cycle with LLMs. However, these focus on system-level robustness (agent workflows, cascading failures) rather than specifically measuring safety guardrail degradation under prompt-level fault injection (truncation, noise, garbled context). The specific contribution — injecting controlled perturbations into prompt components and measuring a safety degradation curve as a function of chaos intensity — is a distinct experimental design not directly published, though the chaos engineering framing for LLM systems is established.
